candidates.rationale: Cholesterol (Hollenhorst) emboli have a highly reflective, glistening yellow-copper appearance. Calcific emboli are chalk-like, whereas fibrin-platelet emboli are dull and elongated.
candidates.stem: Which appearance is characteristic of a cholesterol (Hollenhorst) retinal embolus?

candidates.rationale: Calcific retinal emboli tend to cause more severe obstruction and are typically large, round or ovoid, with a chalk-like appearance. Cholesterol emboli generally do not produce complete obstruction.

sourceCitations.quote: Tend to cause more severe obstructions

candidates.stem: Which type of retinal embolus tends to cause more severe arterial obstruction?

candidates.rationale: Fibrin-platelet emboli are described as dull and elongated and are highly mobile. This differs from the glistening appearance of cholesterol emboli and the chalk-like appearance of calcific emboli.
candidates.stem: Which retinal embolus is described as dull and elongated?

candidates.rationale: Cardiac emboli are usually calcific. This composition reflects the typical embolic material associated with cardiac disease, although other embolus types can occur.
candidates.stem: What type of retinal embolus is usually associated with cardiac disease?

options: Respiratory disease rather than cardiovascular disease
Ocular complications rather than systemic disease
candidates.rationale: The reported comparison is 80% of deaths from cardiovascular disease versus stroke. CRAO therefore signals substantial systemic cardiovascular risk, not only an ocular problem.

sourceCitations.quote: Majority (80%) of patients with CRAO die from cardiovascular disease vs stroke

candidates.stem: Among patients with central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), what accounts for the majority of reported deaths?

candidates.rationale: In BRAO, 75% of patients have presenting visual acuity of 20/40 or better. Visual acuity may remain relatively good when the macula is not involved.

sourceCitations.quote: Presenting VA: 75% of patients are 20/40 or better

candidates.stem: What presenting visual acuity is reported in 75% of patients with branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO)?

candidates.rationale: A retinal embolus can occur without producing retinal infarction, but it still warrants prompt evaluation. The goal is to identify associated vascular or systemic disease and assess future stroke risk.

sourceCitations.quote: If retinal embolus WITHOUT infarction or asymptomatic, newly diagnosed CRAO/BRAO/OAO, recommend prompt evaluation (AAO PPP)

candidates.stem: What is recommended for a retinal embolus without infarction?

correctAnswers: Ipsilateral carotid stenosis of 70–99%, even if asymptomatic
options: Ipsilateral carotid stenosis of 70–99%, even if asymptomatic
Any degree of contralateral carotid stenosis
Ipsilateral carotid stenosis of 10–29% only when asymptomatic
Ipsilateral carotid stenosis of 50–69% only when asymptomatic
candidates.rationale: Carotid endarterectomy is indicated for 70–99% ipsilateral stenosis, including patients without symptoms. Symptomatic patients with 50–69% stenosis may receive a moderate benefit, which is a separate threshold and situation.

sourceCitations.quote: Indicated to prevent stroke in patients who have ipsilateral stenosis 70-99% (even if asymptomatic)

candidates.stem: For retinal arterial emboli, when is carotid endarterectomy indicated to prevent stroke?

candidates.rationale: When conventional cardiovascular risk factors are absent in a young patient, hypercoagulable and primary hematologic disorders become important considerations in the evaluation of retinal emboli.

sourceCitations.quote: Young patients without conventional cardiovascular risk factors – hypercoagulable and primary hematologic disorders

candidates.stem: What additional disorders should be considered in young patients with retinal arterial emboli who lack conventional cardiovascular risk factors?

candidates.rationale: Emboli are systemic vascular causes of transient monocular vision loss. Tear-film abnormalities and macular disease are ocular causes, whereas orbital masses are nonvascular orbital causes.
candidates.stem: Which of the following is classified as a systemic vascular cause of transient monocular vision loss?

candidates.rationale: Orbital masses are categorized as nonvascular orbital causes of transient monocular vision loss. Retinal vasospasm is ocular, while hypoperfusion and vasculitis are systemic vascular causes.
candidates.stem: Which of the following is a nonvascular orbital cause of transient monocular vision loss?

candidates.rationale: Giant cell arteritis is included among the differential diagnoses of painful transient monocular vision loss and requires urgent attention. The other choices are ocular conditions listed as causes of transient monocular vision loss but are not identified in this painful differential.

sourceCitations.quote: Differential diagnoses of PAINFUL transient monocular vision loss
Giant cell arteritis → ts an emergency

candidates.stem: Which condition is included in the differential diagnosis of painful transient monocular vision loss?

correctAnswers: Painful Horner syndrome with contralateral systemic neurologic signs
options: Painful Horner syndrome with contralateral systemic neurologic signs
Painless bilateral visual loss without neurologic signs
Gradual bilateral blurring relieved by blinking
Monocular visual loss occurring only after eye closure
candidates.rationale: Carotid artery dissection can produce transient monocular vision loss along with a painful Horner syndrome and neurologic findings on the opposite side. This combination helps distinguish it from uncomplicated painless embolic episodes.

sourceCitations.quote: Painful Horner's and contralateral systemic neurologic signs

candidates.stem: Which presentation is associated with carotid artery dissection?

correctAnswers: They may occur without retinal infarction, and many affected patients are asymptomatic.
options: They may occur without retinal infarction, and many affected patients are asymptomatic.
They invariably produce retinal infarction and profound visual loss.
They are defined only by emboli originating from the heart.
They always cause permanent loss of the entire visual field.
candidates.rationale: Retinal arterial emboli may occur without an associated retinal infarction, and many patients with retinal emboli are asymptomatic.

sourceCitations.quote: Retinal emboli may not have an associated retinal infarction; many patients with retinal emboli are asymptomatic

candidates.stem: Which statement about retinal arterial emboli is accurate?

candidates.rationale: The three principal retinal arterial embolus types are cholesterol (Hollenhorst), calcific, and fibrin-platelet. Fat, infectious or inflammatory material, talc, silicone, and air are listed as uncommon materials rather than the primary three types.
candidates.stem: Which group contains the three retinal arterial embolus types identified?
